nameStory: The white-striped running crab spider gets its name from the distinctive pale stripes that run along its body, combined with its impressive speed and crab-like sideways movement. Like other running crab spiders, it can scuttle quickly in any direction when threatened, resembling a tiny crab more than a typical spider.
description: The white-striped running crab spider is a small, fast-moving hunter that looks quite different from the web-spinning spiders most people know. These compact spiders have a flattened body and hold their front legs out to the sides like a crab ready to grab prey. They're typically brownish or grayish with characteristic white or pale stripes running lengthwise down their body. Adults are quite small, usually measuring less than half an inch across including their legs.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for distinct white or cream-colored stripes running lengthwise down the brownish body - these pale lines are the spider's signature feature and stand out clearly against the darker background

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The body feels firm and flattened when observed closely, with a crab-like appearance that's wider than it is tall, quite different from the rounded abdomen of orb weavers

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky motions and can run sideways or backwards with surprising speed when disturbed - watch for this distinctive crab-like scuttling movement

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to fit comfortably on a dime, with the body typically measuring around 4-6mm long, though the leg span makes them appear slightly larger

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web at all - these are active hunters that rely on speed and ambush tactics rather than silk traps, though they may leave thin draglines as safety ropes

habitat: Look for white-striped running crab spiders on tree bark, fence posts, and building exteriors throughout New England, where their mottled coloring provides excellent camouflage. They particularly favor rough-textured surfaces like weathered wood or stone walls where they can easily grip and hide in crevices. You'll also find them hunting on flowers and low vegetation in gardens and woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often seen sunning themselves on south-facing surfaces during mild days. This is when you're most likely to spot mating pairs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting during daylight hours. Look for them on flowers where they ambush visiting insects.
seasonality.fall: Adults are still active through early fall, with females guarding their egg sacs under bark or in protected crevices. Activity slows as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs or young spiders hidden under bark, in leaf litter, or other protected locations.

funFact: These spiders can change direction instantly without turning around - they can run full speed backwards or sideways just as easily as forwards, making them nearly impossible for prey to escape once spotted.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small crab spiders, but most crab spiders are rounder and sit motionless on flowers, while running crab spiders are flatter and much more active. Remember: if it's running around quickly, it's probably a running crab spider; if it's sitting perfectly still on a flower, it's likely a regular crab spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crab spiders,' running crab spiders are in a completely different family from the flower crab spiders that most people think of. The name comes purely from their crab-like movement and leg positioning, not from any close evolutionary relationship.
compareHints: The white-striped running crab spider is distinguished from its relatives by those prominent longitudinal white stripes - most other Philodromus species in New England have more subtle markings or different color patterns. The Metallic Crab Spider has a more iridescent sheen, while the Turf Running Spider tends to be more uniformly colored without the distinctive striping.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the White-striped Running Crab Spider which has obvious white stripes, the metallic crab spider males are uniformly shiny without stripes.

The Turf Running Spider differs from its Philodromus relatives primarily in habitat preference - while the Metallic Crab Spider tends toward trees and the White-striped Running Crab Spider prefers taller shrubs, the Turf Running Spider sticks to low vegetation and ground cover.

Compared to other Philodromus species in New England, the Resplendent Running Crab Spider stands out for its particularly brilliant metallic appearance - more lustrous than the Metallic Crab Spider and lacking the white stripes of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.

Among its Philodromus relatives in New England, the male's distinctive shiny black coloration with white edges makes it relatively easy to distinguish from the more uniformly colored Metallic Crab Spider or the striped patterns of the White-striped Running Crab Spider.
The Minute Running Crab Spider is significantly smaller than its relatives like the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, which are much more commonly encountered.
Philodromus exilis is notably more slender than the Metallic Crab Spider or White-striped Running Crab Spider, lacking the metallic sheen or distinct striping of those relatives.
